items.title: Using the stack-frame tests as design-enforcement tool.
items.box:
Using the stack-frame tests as design-enforcement tool.

WHAT EXISTS (paths under spirit/test/)
- tools/wirePaths.js records, during the suites it drives, every call stack inside our own code that reaches a bottom, and ranks the paths. A stack sees where code arrives, not what it resembles, so it finds a second route to the same place even when no name or text is shared.
- Its bottoms: wire (the network), fs-write, crypto, child-process, and two components, presenceNode and postQueue.
- oneDoorStacks.js (goal/G19.14) is the enforcing suite: one test per bottom that names a door. It runs that row's suites and fails on any stack with a production frame (spirit/run/) and no frame in the door. Stacks with no production frame are a suite unit-testing the component and are not counted. A run that never reaches the component fails.
- Two doors are enforced today: nobody but peerPost reaches presenceNode, and nobody but peerPost reaches postQueue.
- oneDoorStacks.js is part of run all: runAll.js and deskVerify's full run both take every suite in spirit/test.

HOW IT ENFORCES A DESIGN
- A design rule of the form "only this door may reach that component" becomes one row: the door, the component, and the suites that drive it.
- The wire, fs-write, crypto and child-process bottoms are measured but have no door yet; each ruling such as "only X writes to disk" costs one row.

ITS LIMIT
- It sees only the paths the driven suites walk: a row is as good as its suites, and a path no suite exercises stays invisible.

ITEMS
- goal/G22.3: the gg plugin, a goal-governance plugin desk mounts from its plugin folder.

items.title: gg plugin: goal governance by a mounted plugin
items.box:
gg plugin: goal governance by a mounted plugin.

DECIDED (Andy, 2026-10-13)
- A gg plugin is a goal-governance plugin: for its type of goal it is the first to handle every desk event, and the mechanical controls it implements live there, not in desk.js.
- No goal-type choice at create-goal: desk scans its plugin folder and mounts every plugin it finds; the first plugin governs stack-frame goals.
- The stack-frame plugin sets the parameters (gate frame and target frame) and generates the equivalent of a goal/G22.2 item from them.
- It governs its goal: the goal always stays open, and its rerun item (as goal/G22.1) always stays open, whether a Done button is ever seen or not.
- It has a companion dialog where the gate and endpoint functions are entered.
- It is a pluggable version of goal/G0: a special goal that is always open while actually closed.
- On its first mount the plugin gets its own private goal with a fixed key, and from then on that goal and the plugin live hand in hand; the goal has its chat, box and everything else for free; its private UI is its tab under Apps.

THIS RENDITION (Andy, 2026-10-13) does only:
- Mount every plugin in desk's plugin folder, organized with the same pattern as shell apps and processes.
- The stackFrameChecks plugin, governing in full in this item: its goal and its rerun item always stay open, and its dialog takes a gate and an endpoint and makes the goal/G22.2-type item.
- A main desk tab, Apps, whose inner tabs are the special goals: Team (today's Team tab, moved into Apps as its first special goal) and Stacks (the stackFrameChecks plugin's private UI), more later. Apps replaces the label button in the List.
- When this item is done, a goal "Maintain this plugin" follows.
- The plugin folder: each plugin's server half at spirit/run/process/js/desk/plugins/js/<name>/<name>.js with its .json beside it, its private UI at spirit/run/shell/desk/plugins/<name>/.

THE DOOR LIST (Andy, 2026-10-13, in plugin/stackFrameChecks; built in this item)
- The plugin keeps the doors in spirit/run/process/js/desk/plugins/js/stackFrameChecks/stackFrameList.json, which the stack-frame test reads to know which checks to run.
- The gate is narrow: one file::function; a whole module named as the gate is cheating. The endpoint is wide: a whole module, every function it exports; for what lies outside our code, such as a relay, Node's own (http, https, fetch), filtered to the relay's paths.
- The stack-frame test, the plugin and its UI are changed to that effect, and the three doors written so far move into the list with their gates narrowed.
- A callback runs on a fresh stack, so the probe uses async_hooks: when a callback is placed it keeps the placer's stack and joins it under the callback's, so the walk reaches the named function that set it up. Test-only; probed runs get slower.
- The probe constructs a complete stack frame for anything that reaches an endpoint: the live stack, the stacks of whoever placed each callback (async_hooks), and for every frame the functions it is written inside (its enclosing functions in the source), so a gate such as peerPost.js::createPeerPost holds for every function created inside it.
- The plugin runs the show: its UI gives the complete toolset, rows added (with validation) and removed, and a run dialog for each door that runs its check and shows the verdict and the paths around the gate.
- Rows can also be modified in place, with the same validation as adding.
- A run shows its violators one line each: file:line function (from its caller) ---> what it reaches at the endpoint, bypassing the gate; one line per distinct violator, with how many calls.
- No silent filters: every entry point is tested, loopback included; an exception to a door is written into it by name and reported in every run, never dropped unseen.
- Each input of the Stacks UI is a block that sits inline: a frame holding the field's name and a one-line explanation, with the input below them.
- goal/G22 is done once the plugin is looped in with the verifier.
- Out of scope here: musings and rules moving into desk apps.
- Every run in Stacks reports to deskVerify: the plugin launches a door's run through deskVerify, and each row shows deskVerify's verdict.
- The plugin commits its own list after each change; that belongs with committing reds.
- The Verify tab shows the detailed results of the current run like a console, cleared before every new run, so every run, the ones from Stacks included, has its output there.

items.title: Hub and offboard reach relays only through peerPost
items.box:
The hub and offboard reach relays only through peerPost.

DECIDED (Andy, 2026-10-13)
- The relay violators the stack-frame doors find are fixed in goal/G22, so its goal run goes green honestly.
- Every request our production code sends to a relay goes through peerPost (the gate peerPost.js::createPeerPost); the stack-frame test is the judge, through deskVerify.
- peerPost owns every contact with a relay, its relaying and its public verbs (key, claim) alike, and uses relayRequest only inside itself; the hub never touches a relay or relayRequest, it asks peerPost. Relay listing is a search over the relays peerPost already knows, with no call to a relay.
- Offboard asks its node, never a relay.
- One door holds it: nothing reaches a relay or relayRequest except through peerPost.js::createPeerPost.
- No exception: since goal/G22.5 the node has its key from boot, so even a post to the node itself before it knows a relay goes through peerPost.

FOUND (the relay door's run, 2026-10-13; paths under spirit/run/)
- js/hub.js:300 sealedClaim, from handleClaim: fetches the relay's key itself.
- js/hub.js:1084 handleClaim: posts the claim to the relay itself.
- js/hub.js:2784 relaySummary, from relayGet and from relaySearch, via ownerBadge's probe: asks each relay for its key itself.
- js/hub.js:2651 handlePartnerCheck: fetches the relay's key itself.
- js/hub.js:1019 withClaimRelay and js/hub.js:1774 handleContact: check a relay's address with the relay library directly.
- process/js/desk/offboard.js:78 main: fetches the relay's key with a plain fetch, around even the relay library.
- peerPost today offers post, onRequest, onReply and its stream functions; none of these fetch a relay's key or send a claim, so peerPost needs those calls of its own.

checks.words: Make the relay accept key and claim requests from unknown signers on its one door as its own item, before G22.4?

chat.text: how do you plan to handle these 7 issues?

Three moves for the seven:
1. Four of them fetch a relay's key or send a claim (the hub's claim, partner check and relay summary, and ownerBadge's probe under it). peerPost gets two calls of its own, relayKey(url) and claim(url, body), and the hub and ownerBadge use them. Then every key fetch and claim leaves through peerPost, and the hub keeps no transport.
2. Two (withClaimRelay, handleContact) only check that a relay address is well-formed: assertRelayUrl sends nothing, it sits in relayRequest.js only by history. It moves to a small module of its own, so the relayRequest door counts transport and nothing else. Your call whether that is honest or a dodge; I think honest, since nothing goes over the wire.
3. Offboard is a separate tool talking to its node. It fetches the key only to address its goodbye; it should ask its node instead. If no existing verb gives a relay's key, that needs a new node verb, which is yours to approve with a review.
The red first: the doors as they stand already fail on all seven, so the red is the current oneDoorStacks run; done when the relay doors run green in deskVerify.
1. in english

1, in plain words: today the hub talks to relays itself in four places, when someone claims a name, when it checks a partner, and when it lists relays, each time asking a relay for its key or handing it a claim. Instead, peerPost learns to do those two things (ask a relay for its key, hand a relay a claim), and the hub asks peerPost to do them. Then the hub never talks to a relay on its own, and peerPost is the only part of the node that does.

listing relays must be a normal peerPost(), a search no?
can the claim stuff be handled via the proxy?

Listing: yes, it should be a search, and it needs no relay call at all. peerPost already knows each relay it holds a stream to, with its key and status (relaysHeld, relayStatus); the list becomes a search over what peerPost knows, and the hub's live key fetch per relay goes away.
Claim via the proxy: I'd say no. The proxy is net.fetch, the owner's gate for calls to outside sites; a claim is relay traffic, so sending it there moves the bypass from the hub to net.fetch instead of closing it. The claim belongs inside peerPost, beside post.
relay traffic is peerPosts, the public, non peerPost verbs exists on the relay as well, outside it's actual work or relaying

Then I had it wrong, and your proxy idea fits. A relay has two kinds of door: its work, relaying (post, reply, stream), which is peerPost's; and its public verbs (its key, a claim, its version), which are a public web service like any other site, so they go through the proxy, net.fetch, under your allow list.
So the rule becomes: every call to a relay goes through exactly one of two roads, peerPost for relaying and the proxy for its public verbs, and nothing else may reach a relay. The hub's key fetches and claim, and offboard's fetch, move onto the proxy.
For the doors: two rows on the network, one gated at peerPost for the relaying routes, one gated at the proxy for the public ones, and any call on neither road is a violator. Is that the shape?
and any old donkey can call those relay verbs without our core's permission, so why not us?

We may, the relay does not care who asks. The one-door rule was never about the relay's permission; it is about us having one road, so there is one timeout, one size cap, one place to fix a fault. The review's M11 (relayRequest has no timeout and no size cap) is exactly what a second road hides.
So for the public verbs, the honest door is the one transport: the hub calling them through relayRequest is fine, and only a call around it is a violator. That leaves one real violator for this class, offboard's plain fetch; the hub's four become legal.
The relaying routes (post, reply, stream) stay peerPost's alone. Two rows, then: relaying gated at peerPost, public relay verbs gated at relayRequest. Agreed?
why do you want the hub to reach into peerRequest?

I don't, on reflection: that was me bending to "any donkey may call them". The hub reaching into relayRequest is the hub keeping a transport of its own, which is what we are removing.
The clean shape is the first plan: the hub never touches a relay or its transport; it asks peerPost. peerPost owns every contact with a relay, relaying and public verbs alike, and uses relayRequest inside itself; relay listing is a search over the relays peerPost already knows.
Then one door covers it all: nothing reaches a relay or relayRequest except through createPeerPost, and offboard asks its node rather than the relay. Go with that?
the only legal loophole i can see would be a peerPeer post to the very own node, before it knows a relay.

Recorded in the box (v3): peerPost owns every contact with a relay, listing is a search over what it knows, offboard asks its node, one door at createPeerPost, and your one exception, a post to the node itself before it knows a relay, named in the door and reported every run. I take the red on your Go.
explain in detail.

The plan in detail.

Today: the hub talks to relays on its own in four places, and offboard in one.
- Claim: when someone claims a name on a relay, the hub first asks the relay for its key, then sends the claim itself.
- Partner check: the hub asks a relay for its key itself.
- Relay list (relay.get and relay.search): the hub asks every relay for its key and status itself, through ownerBadge's probe, to show which relays are online and joined.
- Contact and claim-relay addresses: the hub checks a relay address with the relay library directly (only a format check, nothing sent).
- Offboard: the tool fetches a relay's key with a plain web request, around everything.

After:
1. peerPost gets two new abilities of its own: ask a relay for its key, and hand a relay a claim. They use the relay library inside peerPost, with its one timeout and size limit.
2. The hub's claim and partner check ask peerPost for those, and stop calling the relay library.
3. The relay list stops asking relays live. peerPost already holds a stream to each relay it uses and knows each one's key and state; the list becomes a search over that. A relay peerPost has never met shows as not joined, not as probed.
4. The address check moves out of the relay library into a small module of its own, since it sends nothing; then "the relay library" means only things that go over the wire.
5. Offboard asks its own node for the relay's key with relay.get, an existing verb that already answers it, so no new node verb is needed.
6. The one exception you named, a post to the node itself before it knows any relay, is written into the door by name and shows in every run as excepted.

The judge: the relay door, gated at createPeerPost with no path filter, run through deskVerify. It is red today on these paths; the item is done when that door is green, except for the named exception.
The risk: the relay list changes what it shows for relays peerPost has no stream to; that is the one visible change for you.
Does the Node now finally generate it ID-key on first boot?

No. A node's key is still made at its first claim, not at boot: hub.js signedClaim calls ensureIdentity (hub.js line 158), and server.js never calls it on start. A relay does make its key on boot (relayServer.js line 385); a node does not.
So a fresh node has no key until it claims a name, which is also why your exception exists: before it knows a relay it has nothing to sign with.
Making the node mint its key on first boot is a small change of its own; say so and I add it as an item.

FUCK! i thought we fixed that. This is SOOOOOO stupid. Fix that now, before anything else. god, how many times do we go through this shit.

explain! no code.

I was wrong a moment ago, and it is worse than "not at boot". Checked in a scratch folder just now:
1. On first boot the node does make a key (server.js calls ensureIdentity with an empty name, since 2026-09-24).
2. But that key is saved without a name, and loadIdentity, which everything uses to read the node's key, refuses an identity with no name, so the node acts as if it had no key.
3. At the first claim, ensureIdentity looks with loadIdentity, finds "nothing", and makes a NEW key over the boot one. Measured: boot key ...W3SSLiKaqYE=, after the claim ...Os4xtEVX27A=.
So the key is made at boot and thrown away at the first claim; the node's real identity still begins at its claim. The boot key was added for a different reason (old nodes growing a seal key) and nobody joined it to the claim path.
The fix: a key needs no name. loadIdentity accepts a nameless identity, the claim keeps the key it finds and only writes the name, and a test pins it: boot, claim, same key.
now why the fuck would that first key be thrown away? god, this is stupid?

No good reason; two changes that never met.
On 2026-09-13 "has an identity" was written as "has a name and a key", because then both were made together, at the claim (relayAuth.js loadIdentity: no name, no identity).
On 2026-09-24 the boot step was added to grow a seal key on old nodes; on a fresh node it also makes a key, with an empty name. Nobody changed the 09-13 definition, so that key fails it, and the claim, seeing "no identity", makes another.
The name is not part of the identity; the key is. That is the fix.
the first call to ensureIdentity MUST fucking ensure a real, permanent identity exists. Ensure Identity can take the machine-name as a default, it's not rocket science. New item EnsureIdentity.
Opened goal/G22.5, "EnsureIdentity": the first call makes the one permanent identity, the machine name is the default name, and it goes before anything else. Ready on your Go and code.
how is this situation changed based on the changes done in 22.5?

The seven violators themselves are unchanged: they are about which road reaches a relay, not about the key.
Two things did change:
1. The exception you named (a post to the node itself before it knows a relay) existed because a fresh node had nothing to sign with. Now it has its key from boot, so that post can go through peerPost like any other; I'd drop the exception unless a measured run still shows it.
2. The claim no longer makes a key, it only names the node. So moving the claim into peerPost is clean: peerPost always holds the identity, and the hub's claim no longer has a "no identity yet" case to carry along.

exception dropped.

now i want, again, every hub-grope past peerPost explained.

Exception dropped, recorded. Every place the hub goes past peerPost, what it does, and where it goes after the fix:
1. Claiming a name (handleClaim, hub.js 1068, with sealedClaim at 300). The hub asks the relay for its key (GET /api/relay/key), seals the claim to that key, then sends the claim itself (POST /api/relay/claim). Two calls, both its own. After: peerPost.claim(url, name, invite) does both; the hub only hands over the request and reads the answer.
2. Checking the claim relay's address (withClaimRelay, hub.js 1015). Before claiming, the hub checks the address is https (or loopback http) with the relay library. Nothing is sent. After: the check moves to its own small module; it is not a road to a relay.
3. Adding a contact (handleContact, hub.js 1771). Same address check on the contact's relay, nothing sent. After: same small module.
4. Checking a partner (handlePartnerCheck, hub.js 2620). To tell who runs a relay, the hub asks the relay for its key and reads its ownerKey. After: peerPost.relayKey(url) answers it, the same call the claim uses.
5. Listing relays (relaySummary, hub.js 2783, for relay.get and relay.search, through ownerBadge's probe). For the list, the hub asks every relay live for its key and status. After: no call at all; the list is a search over the relays peerPost already holds streams to, with their keys and state.
Offboard, outside the hub: it fetches the key by plain fetch; after, it asks its node with relay.get.

if the hub can't do that through peerPost, getRelayKey etc... then there is something wrong with the relay.

the relay accepts "public" requests through and extra door? but it cannot allow "unknown" keys in answer Self to have the same leeway?

That is the root, yes. The relay's real door (post and reply) refuses any signer it does not know, so a stranger cannot even ask "who are you" or "let me in" there; the public routes (key, claim) are the side door that was cut for exactly those two questions.
The fix you describe: the relay's one door accepts a signed packet from an unknown key, but only for those two things, its key and a claim, answered like any reply and counted against the stranger's rate. Then the hub asks through peerPost like everything else, and the public routes close.
It changes the wire, so it is a flag day for every relay and node, and it is relay work, not hub work. Make it its own item ahead of G22.4, and G22.4 then only moves the hub onto it?

items.title: EnsureIdentity
items.box:
EnsureIdentity: one real identity from the first call.

DECIDED (Andy, 2026-10-13)
- The first call to ensureIdentity ensures a real, permanent identity exists; every later call returns that same identity and never makes another.
- When no name is given, ensureIdentity takes the machine's name as the default.
- This is fixed before anything else in goal/G22.
- The node calls ensureIdentity during boot, first, before the hub is made, so the hub never has a chance or a need to make one; the claim finds the identity already there.
- Law: no node-boot is done until the node has a key and a default name.

items.box:
Relay answers unknown IDs asking for public services.

DECIDED (Andy, 2026-10-13)
- The fix belongs in the relay: it corrects how a relay answers an unknown ID that wants its public services.
- The relay's one door accepts a signed request from a key it does not know, for its public services only (its key, a claim), answers it like any reply, and is held to the address table below; so a node reaches a relay only through peerPost, and the public side routes close.
- This blocks goal/G22.4: once it lands, the hub asks peerPost for a relay's key and for a claim.
- The door first looks at packets addressed to the relay itself: one from an unknown key is read and answered if it is the card ask (answered with the relay's key) or a claim, and refused otherwise; only packets for others need a known sender.
- One plaintext exception stays, the card ask; there is no separate key request.
- The relay's public door, the one any curl can reach without key or signature, is killed in this item: /api/relay/key, /api/relay/claim, /api/version and the brochure all close. The relay keeps its one door (post) and its members' stream.
- Every comment and document that mentions the killed door (the public routes, claims redeemed there, curl checks of /api/version or /api/relay/key) is corrected in this item as well.
- Partnering as a permission goes, in this item: a relay carries posts to its members from any relay, the member's one slot in flight counted per sender (the October 10 review's M5) so no stranger can keep a member busy; the partner roll and the partner budget are removed; design/relay/PARTNERS.md is reduced to a dated record of its own obsolescence.
- Strangers are held by one table of requesting addresses, as many entries as the relay has members, each entry: request count, time of last request, originating address, ban time (starting at 1000 ms). An address that asks again before its ban time is over has its ban time doubled. A new address takes the first expired slot; when none is expired, its request is refused as busy. The table lives in memory only; nothing about a stranger is written to disk. An address that comes back after its ban ended starts again at 1 s, since a thousand users may sit behind one address. An IPv6 address is counted by its /64 block, since one machine owns the whole block. The first request from an unknown ID is answered and puts that ID's address into the table; only a repeat is held to the ban. If the table is full with nothing expired, that first request is refused with the error busy. It replaces the per-address claim limit.
- A stranger addresses the relay itself with an empty target (to: ""), since it does not know the relay's key yet; a stranger's post has the same size limit as any post.
- The claim keeps its inner signature, so the claim itself does not change shape.
- bash/status, which checked a relay with curl, checks it with a small node script that sends the card ask instead.

A "stranger" is a key the relay does not know. Anyone can make a new key in a millisecond, for free, as many as they like.
